newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's new top judge backs Yeltsin constitution.
newsitem.headline: Russia's new top judge backs Yeltsin constitution.

text.p: The new chairman of Russia's Constitutional Court said on Thursday he would resist changes in the country's basic law advocated by political opponents of President Boris Yeltsin.
"The constitution is a very icon among laws which should not be changed," Marat Baglai, 66, told reporters after the 19- member court elected him its new chairman.
He was referring to a remark by the chairman of the Federation Council upper chamber of parliament that the constitution was not sacrosanct and should be amended.
"The constitution secures stability of power and it is unreasonable to break it," said Baglai, a career lawyer who replaces retiring Vladimir Tumanov.

Yeltsin, who dissolved the Soviet-era parliament in 1993, made sure that the new constitution approved through a referendum later that year granted him sweeping powers to push ahead with political and economic reforms.

But the poor health of the 66-year-old Kremlin leader, who has hardly spent a month in his Kremlin office since his re-election last June and who had heart surgery last November, has prompted opposition calls to shift the balance of power towards other institutions.
Yeltsin himself has rejected such proposals and has said he is fit to serve out his four-year term.
A long, multi-stage procedure makes constitutional changes unlikely unless they are backed by all major political forces.
The position of the Constitutional Court, a body specially set up to interpret the basic law, would further complicate matters for the opposition if it decided to push ahead with changes.
